text.content: Not every request Cascadia's support system receives has a natural sequence. When a customer submits a message that touches multiple domains at once — a delayed shipment with a warranty question about the delayed product — Sofia does not want the workflow to check shipping first, then wait, then check warranty. Both checks can run at the same time, and their results can be combined into one response at the end. This is what parallel orchestration is for: independent agents working simultaneously on different angles of the same request, then merging their findings.

text.content: Parallel orchestration in a nutshell

rich_text.plain_text: Parallel orchestration in a nutshell

text.content: A parallel workflow sends the same request, or different parts of a request, to multiple agents at once and then combines their outputs into one final result.

rich_text.plain_text: A parallel workflow sends the same request, or different parts of a request, to multiple agents at once and then combines their outputs into one final result.

text.content: In a sequential workflow, each step depends on the previous step. Agent B waits for Agent A. Agent C waits for Agent B. This is useful when the task has a clear chain of dependency.

rich_text.plain_text: In a sequential workflow, each step depends on the previous step. Agent B waits for Agent A. Agent C waits for Agent B. This is useful when the task has a clear chain of dependency.

text.content: In a parallel workflow, the agents do not wait for each other during their main work. Each agent receives its assignment, completes it independently, and returns a result. A final coordination step then compares, combines, or prioritizes those results.

text.content: Why parallel workflows are useful

rich_text.plain_text: Why parallel workflows are useful

text.content: Parallel orchestration is useful when a task has several independent angles. Instead of asking one agent to think about everything, you assign different responsibilities to different agents.

rich_text.plain_text: Parallel orchestration is useful when a task has several independent angles. Instead of asking one agent to think about everything, you assign different responsibilities to different agents.

text.content: This can improve speed, because several agents work at the same time. It can also improve quality, because each agent focuses on one type of reasoning. A risk agent can look for weak points, a business agent can focus on value, and a technical agent can focus on feasibility.

text.content: The key word is independent. Parallel orchestration works best when each agent can do meaningful work without needing another agent’s output first.

text.content: A parallel workflow usually has four parts.

text.content: Second, there is a splitter. The splitter decides which agents should receive which part of the work. Sometimes every agent receives the same full input. Sometimes each agent receives a specific subtask.

text.content: A good parallel task has three qualities.

rich_text.plain_text: A good parallel task has three qualities.

text.content: The agents can work independently. One agent does not need another agent’s result before starting.

rich_text.plain_text: The agents can work independently. One agent does not need another agent’s result before starting.

text.content: The outputs are complementary. Each agent adds a different perspective, rather than repeating the same work.

rich_text.plain_text: The outputs are complementary. Each agent adds a different perspective, rather than repeating the same work.

text.content: The results can be merged. There is a clear way to combine the outputs into a final decision, summary, or recommendation.

text.content: If these three qualities are missing, parallel orchestration may create more confusion than value.

text.content: What should not run in parallel?

text.content: Do not use parallel orchestration when the task has strong dependencies.

rich_text.plain_text: Do not use parallel orchestration when the task has strong dependencies.

text.content: For example, if one agent must first extract customer requirements and another agent must then build a solution based on those requirements, this is not a good parallel flow. The second agent needs the first agent’s output. That is sequential orchestration.

text.content: Parallel orchestration is also risky when agents are allowed to make overlapping decisions without a merge rule. If three agents each produce a different final recommendation and no agent is responsible for resolving the disagreement, the workflow becomes unreliable.

text.content: Parallel orchestration is not about adding agents for variety. It is about splitting work where the split creates value. If two agents are likely to produce the same answer, they probably should not both be in the workflow. If their outputs cannot be merged clearly, the workflow may become harder to debug.

text.content: Summary

rich_text.plain_text: Summary

text.content: Parallel orchestration is useful when a task can be divided into independent parts that benefit from different perspectives. The main design challenge is not only starting multiple agents at once, but also bringing their outputs back together in a reliable way.
